article.title: The growth of bike-sharing schemes around the world

items.sentence_raw: The original idea for an urban bike-sharing scheme dates back to a summer's day in Amsterdam in 1965.
Provo, the organisation that came up with the idea, was a group of Dutch activists who wanted to change society.
items.explain: Q23: The passage says Provo was *'a group of Dutch activists who wanted to change society'*. The people in the group were **activists**. So the answer is **activists**.

items.sentence_raw: They believed the scheme, which was known as the Witte Fietsenplan, was an answer to the perceived threats of air pollution and consumerism.
items.explain:
Q18: The question asks what **problems** the scheme was meant to solve. In paragraph A, the group believed the scheme was *'an answer to the perceived threats of air pollution and consumerism'*. **'An answer to'** means a solution for, and **'threats'** are the problems. The answer is **A**.

Q24: The passage says they were concerned about *'the perceived threats of air pollution and consumerism'*. **'Air pollution'** is damage to the environment, and the other concern was **consumerism**. So the answer is **consumerism**.

items.sentence_raw: In the centre of Amsterdam, they painted a small number of used bikes white.
They also distributed leaflets describing the dangers of cars and inviting people to use the white bikes.
items.explain: Q25: The passage says *'They also distributed leaflets describing the dangers of cars'*. **'Distributed'** means they handed them out. So the answer is **leaflets**.

items.sentence_raw: The bikes were then left unlocked at various locations around the city, to be used by anyone in need of transport.
Luud Schimmelpennink, a Dutch industrial engineer who still lives and cycles in Amsterdam, was heavily involved in the original scheme.
He recalls how the scheme succeeded in attracting a great deal of attention - particularly when it came to publicising Provo's aims - but struggled to get off the ground.
The police were opposed to Provo's initiatives and almost as soon as the white bikes were distributed around the city, they removed them.
items.explain: Q26: The passage says *'The police were opposed to Provo's initiatives and almost as soon as the white bikes were distributed around the city, they removed them'*. So it was the **police** who took the bikes away. The answer is **police**.

items.sentence_raw: However, for Schimmelpennink and for bike-sharing schemes in general, this was just the beginning.
"The first Witte Fietsenplan was just a symbolic thing," he says.
"We painted a few bikes white, that was all.
Things got more serious when I became a member of the Amsterdam city council two years later."
Schimmelpennink seized this opportunity to present a more elaborate Witte Fietsenplan to the city council.
"My idea was that the municipality of Amsterdam would distribute 10,000 white bikes over the city, for everyone to use," he explains.
"I made serious calculations.
It turned out that a white bicycle - per person, per kilometre - would cost the municipality only 10% of what it contributed to public transport per person per kilometre."
items.explain: Q17: The question asks about **potential savings**, which means money you don't have to spend. In paragraph C, Schimmelpennink's calculation showed a white bike *'would cost the municipality only 10% of what it contributed to public transport'*. That's a huge saving. The answer is **C**.

items.sentence_raw: Nevertheless, the council unanimously rejected the plan.
items.explain: Q15: The question asks why a plan was **turned down**, which means rejected. In paragraph C, the council *'unanimously rejected the plan'* because they said *'the bicycle belongs to the past'* and saw a *'glorious future for the car'*. So the answer is **C**.

items.sentence_raw: But he was not in the least discouraged.
Schimmelpennink never stopped believing in bike-sharing, and in the mid-90s, two Danes asked for his help to set up a system in Copenhagen.
The result was the world's first large-scale bike-share programme.
It worked on a deposit: "You dropped a coin in the bike and when you returned it, you got your money back."
After setting up the Danish system, Schimmelpennink decided to try his luck again in the Netherlands - and this time he succeeded in arousing the interest of the Dutch Ministry of Transport.
"Times had changed," he recalls.
"People had become more environmentally conscious, and the Danish experiment had proved that bike-sharing was a real possibility."
items.explain: Q19: The question asks about the 1999 Amsterdam scheme. Paragraph D says *'People had become more environmentally conscious'*, which is a **change in people's attitudes**. This change made the scheme possible. So one correct answer is **D**.

items.sentence_raw: A new Witte Fietsenplan was launched in 1999 in Amsterdam.
However, riding a white bike was no longer free; it cost one guilder per trip and payment was made with a chip card developed by the Dutch bank Postbank.
Schimmelpennink designed conspicuous, sturdy white bikes locked in special racks which could be opened with the chip card - the plan started with 250 bikes, distributed over five stations.
Theo Molenaar, who was a system designer for the project, worked alongside Schimmelpennink.
"I remember when we were testing the bike racks, he announced that he had already designed better ones.
But of course, we had to go through with the ones we had."
The system, however, was prone to vandalism and theft.
"After every weekend there would always be a couple of bikes missing," Molenaar says.
items.explain: Q14: You might think 'misused' means something like breaking the bikes, but look at paragraph E. It says *'After every weekend there would always be a couple of bikes missing'* and *'I really have no idea what people did with them'*. So the misuse was that bikes **disappeared** — people took them. The answer is **E**.

items.sentence_raw: "I really have no idea what people did with them, because they could instantly be recognised as white bikes."

So the misuse was that bikes **disappeared** — people took them. The answer is **E**.

items.sentence_raw: But the biggest blow came when Postbank decided to abolish the chip card, because it wasn't profitable.
items.explain: Q20: For the second correct answer, look at paragraph E. The scheme failed when Postbank *'decided to abolish the chip card'* and the *'business partner had lost interest'*. This means a **partner withdrew support**. So the other correct answer is **B**.

items.sentence_raw: "That chip card was pivotal to the system," Molenaar says.
"To continue the project we would have needed to set up another system, but the business partner had lost interest."

items.sentence_raw: Schimmelpennink was disappointed, but - characteristically - not for long.
In 2002 he got a call from the French advertising corporation JC Decaux, who wanted to set up his bike-sharing scheme in Vienna.
"That went really well.
After Vienna, they set up a system in Lyon.
Then in 2007, Paris followed.
That was a decisive moment in the history of bike-sharing."

The huge and unexpected success of the Parisian bike-sharing programme, which now boasts more than 20,000 bicycles, inspired cities all over the world to set up their own schemes, all modelled on Schimmelpennink's.
"It's wonderful that this happened," he says.
"But financially I didn't really benefit from it, because I never filed for a patent."
items.explain: Q16: The question is about someone who could not **profit** from their work. In paragraph F, Schimmelpennink says *'financially I didn't really benefit from it, because I never filed for a patent'*. **'Didn't benefit'** means he made no money, so he was **unable to profit**. The answer is **F**.

items.sentence_raw: In Amsterdam today, 38% of all trips are made by bike and, along with Copenhagen, it is regarded as one of the two most cycle-friendly capitals in the world - but the city never got another Witte Fietsenplan.
items.explain: Q22: For the second correct answer, paragraph G also says Amsterdam is *'regarded as one of the two most cycle-friendly capitals in the world'*. This means the city has a **reputation as a place that welcomes cyclists**. So the other correct answer is **E**.

items.sentence_raw: Molenaar believes this may be because everybody in Amsterdam already has a bike.
Schimmelpennink, however, cannot see that this changes Amsterdam's need for a bike-sharing scheme.
"People who travel on the underground don't carry their bikes around.
items.explain: Q21: The question asks about Amsterdam today. Paragraph G says people on the underground *'often need additional transport to reach their final destination'*. This means a bike-sharing scheme would help **residents who use public transport**. So one correct answer is **D**.

items.sentence_raw: Although he thinks it is strange that a city like Amsterdam does not have a successful bike-sharing scheme, he is optimistic about the future.
"In the '60s we didn't stand a chance because people were prepared to give their lives to keep cars in the city.
But that mentality has totally changed.
Today everybody longs for cities that are not dominated by cars."
